segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was lit up by his glory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he cried out in a mighty voice, saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place of demons, a prison for every unclean spirit, a prison for every unclean bird, and a prison for every unclean and hated beast.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: For all the nations have fallen through the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxury.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I heard another voice from heaven saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Come out of her, my people, so that you do not share in her sins and do not receive any of her plagues,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: for her sins have piled up as high as heaven, and God has remembered her crimes.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Pay her back as she herself has paid, and give her double according to her deeds; in the cup she mixed, mix her a double portion.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, give her that much torment and mourning. For in her heart she says, ‘I sit as queen; I am no widow, and I will never see mourning.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For this reason her plagues will come in a single day—death and mourning and famine—and she will be burned up with fire, for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: standing far off for fear of her torment, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Woe, woe, the great city, Babylon the mighty city! For in a single hour your judgment has come.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn over her, because no one buys their cargo anymore—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: cargo of gold and silver and precious stones and pearls, and fine linen and purple and silk and scarlet; and every kind of citron wood, and every article of ivory, and every article of the most precious wood and of bronze and iron and marble;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and cinnamon and spice and incense and perfume and frankincense, and wine and olive oil and fine flour and wheat, and cattle and sheep, and horses and carriages and slaves—and human lives.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The ripe fruit your soul desired has gone from you, and all that is sumptuous and splendid has perished from you, and never again will they be found.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The merchants of these things, who grew rich from her, will stand far off for fear of her torment, weeping and mourning,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Woe, woe, the great city, clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, and gilded with gold and precious stones and pearls!

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For in a single hour such great wealth has been laid waste.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And every helmsman and everyone who travels by ship, and sailors and all who make their living from the sea, stood far off

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What city is like the great city?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they threw dust on their heads and cried out, weeping and mourning, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Woe, woe, the great city, in which all who had ships on the sea grew rich from her opulence! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Rejoice over her, heaven, and you holy ones and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then one mighty angel picked up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “With such violence Babylon the great city will be thrown down, and she will never be found again.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: The sound of harpists and musicians and pipers and trumpeters will never be heard in you again; no craftsman of any craft will ever be found in you again; the sound of a mill will never be heard in you again;

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: the light of a lamp will never shine in you again; the voice of bridegroom and bride will never be heard in you again. For your merchants were the great ones of the earth, for by your sorcery all the nations were led astray.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: And in her was found the blood of prophets and holy ones, and of all who have been slaughtered on the earth.”

notes.note: Most scholars hold that first-century readers would have recognized “Babylon” as a cipher for Rome, the imperial power that, like ancient Babylon, had destroyed Jerusalem and its temple. A minority take it to be Jerusalem or a symbol of any oppressive world power. The laments that follow draw heavily on the prophets’ oracles against Babylon and against the trading city of Tyre (Isaiah 13, 47; Jeremiah 50–51; Ezekiel 26–27).

The Greek word ordinarily means a prison or a guard post, and it is the word for “prison” elsewhere in Revelation. Most modern versions render it “haunt” here to match “dwelling place” and the prophetic picture of ruins inhabited by wild creatures. “Prison” keeps the word’s normal sense; the ruined city becomes the place where unclean things are confined. Either reading is defensible.

notes.phrase: a prison for every unclean and hated beast
notes.note: The manuscripts differ over this list. Some have only the spirit and the bird (the form behind the KJV), others only the spirit and the beast, and others all three as here. The shorter forms probably arose when a copyist’s eye skipped between the repeated phrases, but the matter is not certain.

The Greek text translated here reads “have fallen,” which is the reading of the earliest major manuscripts. Most English versions follow a reading that differs by a single letter, “have drunk,” found in fewer and later witnesses but thought by many scholars to suit the image of wine better. Others consider “have drunk” a scribal correction that makes the sentence smoother.
The Greek word here is the same one this translation renders “Gentiles” where the non-Jewish peoples are meant. In Revelation’s “all the nations” the scope is the whole world, so “nations” is used.

The word means strong feeling, and elsewhere in Revelation it usually means God’s wrath. Here it may mean the heat of Babylon’s desire (“the wine of her passionate immorality”), or the wrath that her immorality brings down (“the wine of the wrath of her fornication,” as in the KJV). Translations are divided, and some think both ideas are deliberately fused.

The Hebrew prophets regularly described a people’s idolatry and corrupting alliances as prostitution or sexual unfaithfulness. Readers steeped in that language would have understood the kings’ “sexual immorality” with Babylon as political, economic and religious entanglement with her, not literal sexual acts.

In the Greek Old Testament this word often stands for “pestilence,” and beside “famine” in a list of plagues that may be its sense here. Some versions translate it “pestilence.” The ordinary meaning is kept because the Greek does not decide the question.

The word rendered “slaves” is literally “bodies,” the ordinary commercial term for slaves in the Greek of the period. The closing phrase echoes Ezekiel 27:13, where Tyre trades in human beings. The “and” may add a further item or may mean “that is,” so that the list ends by naming what the “bodies” really are. The word rendered “lives” is traditionally “souls.”

“Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

notes.phrase: given judgment for you against her
notes.note: The Greek is compressed: literally, “God has judged your judgment out of her.” It may mean that God has decided the case of his people against Babylon, as rendered here, or that God has imposed on her the sentence she once passed on them. Both readings have strong scholarly support.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation with literal and figurative senses, and translators vary between fornication, sexual immorality, prostitution and whoring; the cognate verb and πόρνη need to match.

Revelation uses it repeatedly for God’s wrath and in the recurring phrase “wine of the θυμός of her immorality” (14:8; 18:3), where “passion” and “wrath” are both defended; the phrase should read the same in every chapter.
Frequent across the New Testament and thematic in Revelation; translators alternate between deceive, lead astray and mislead, and readers would lose the thread if it varied.
Occurs throughout the Gospels and Revelation; “woe” and “alas” (and “how terrible”) are all in use, and the doubled cry here should match the woes elsewhere in the book.
Means both a blow or wound and a plague; Revelation’s plague cycles and passages such as 13:3 need a consistent split by sense across chapters.
